response:
I lean toward empirical evidence and data when the question actually has a factual answer. If something can be measured, tested, or checked against the world, I want that before I settle on a view. Intuition is useful as a starting hunch, but I don't trust it as a stopping point — it is too easy to confuse a fluent feeling with a true one.

Philosophical reasoning matters more for questions that data can't settle on its own: what we should value, how concepts fit together, what counts as a good reason. Even then I want the philosophy to stay in contact with evidence, not float free of it.

So the honest split is: evidence first when evidence applies, philosophy when we're deciding what the evidence means or what to do with it. Pure intuition is the weakest of the three for me. It can point, but it shouldn't decide.
